sub: Named after “the private rooms” of the Prophet’s ﷺ wives in ayah 4
theme: The manners of true believers: first with Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, then with each other. Check news, make peace, drop mockery, suspicion and backbiting, measure honour by taqwā, and let real faith settle in the heart.
story: Revealed in Madinah, mostly near the end of the Prophet’s ﷺ life. It gathers rulings sent down on different occasions, placed together because they share one subject: the manners worthy of true believers.

The opening ayat are reportedly tied to the Banū Tamīm delegation of 9 AH. Abū Bakr and ʿUmar raised their voices arguing over the tribe’s leader, and some of the visitors shouted for the Prophet ﷺ from outside his wives’ rooms.

Other reports link ayah 6 to a false alarm about Banū al-Muṣṭaliq refusing zakah, and the closing ayat to bedouins, reportedly of Banū Asad, who claimed full faith and acted as if their Islam were a favour to the Prophet ﷺ.

sections.title: Manners with the Prophet ﷺ: don’t rush ahead, lower voices, wait outside
sections.meaning: Don’t put your views ahead of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ; follow his lead. Don’t raise your voice above his or speak to him loudly as you do to each other, or your deeds may be wasted unnoticed. Those who lower their voices are praised; those shouting outside his rooms should have waited.
points: Don’t rush ahead of Allah and His Messenger; fear Allah
Don’t raise your voices over his, or your deeds may be lost
Those who lower their voices: hearts tested for taqwā, forgiveness, great reward
Calling from behind the rooms is senseless; waiting would have been better
sections.matters: It sets the order of the whole surah: manners with Allah and His Messenger ﷺ come first, then manners with people. The warning is sharp: careless disrespect can wipe out deeds without a person even noticing.
sections.story: Reportedly revealed when a Banū Tamīm delegation came. Abū Bakr and ʿUmar argued over who should lead the tribe until their voices rose. Some of the delegation also shouted, “O Muḥammad, come out to us!” from outside his rooms while he rested.
explained: Lā tuqaddimū: don’t step ahead of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ in word or deed. Don’t decide or speak before he does; follow his lead. Allah hears what you say and knows what you intend. Next: don’t speak over him, or call him loudly as you call each other. That disrespect could quietly ruin your deeds.

When it came down, ʿUmar spoke so softly the Prophet ﷺ had to ask him to repeat. Those who lower their voices have hearts Allah has tested and purified for taqwā. Then the bedouins who shouted from behind the ḥujurāt, his wives’ rooms: most had no sense. Waiting until he came out would have been better, and Allah forgives.
teaches: Don’t put your own opinion ahead of what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ said.
Respect for the Prophet ﷺ is part of taqwā.
A careless word or tone can cost deeds without you noticing.
Good manners are a sign of good sense; patient waiting beats shouting.
sections.hook: Ayat 1 and 2 both open “O you who have believed, do not…”. Voices are raised in 2 and lowered in 3. Ayah 4 names the surah: al-ḥujurāt.

sections.title: Verify news before acting; when believers fight, make peace between brothers justly
sections.meaning: If a fāsiq, a sinful person, brings news, verify it before acting, or you may harm innocent people and regret it. The Messenger ﷺ is among you; if he followed your wishes you would suffer. If two groups of believers fight, make peace; fight the aggressor until it returns, then settle justly. Believers are brothers.
points: A fāsiq brings news? Verify first, or you’ll harm people and regret it
The Messenger is among you; Allah made faith beloved, a favour from Him
Two believing groups fight: reconcile; fight the aggressor until it returns; be just
Believers are brothers, so make peace between them and fear Allah
sections.matters: The surah moves from manners with the Prophet ﷺ to life among believers. Rumours and fighting tear a community apart, so it starts with two protections: check the news before acting, and make just peace when believers clash.
sections.story: Ayah 6 reportedly came after al-Walīd ibn ʿUqbah mistakenly reported that Banū al-Muṣṭaliq had refused zakah and meant to kill him; a check found them praying and obedient. Ayah 9 reportedly followed a scuffle between two groups of Muslims with palm stalks, hands and sandals.
explained: Fatabayyanū: verify. When news comes from a fāsiq, someone whose word can’t be trusted, don’t act on it at once. Check it, or you may strike innocent people in ignorance and wake up regretting it. Know that Allah’s Messenger ﷺ is among you. If he went along with your opinions in many matters, you would fall into hardship and sin.

But Allah made faith beloved to you and beautiful in your hearts, and made disbelief, sin and disobedience hateful. That is His favour. If two groups of believers fight, reconcile them. If one keeps attacking, fight it until it returns to Allah’s command, then make peace with fairness. Believers are brothers, so mend things between them.
teaches: Check news before you act on it, especially from unreliable people.
Trust the Prophet’s ﷺ guidance over your own quick reactions.
Loving faith and hating sin is a gift from Allah.
When believers quarrel, don’t take sides blindly; make peace with justice.
Believers are brothers, wherever they live.
sections.hook: Ayah 6 is the surah’s third “O you who have believed.” Fa-aṣliḥū, “make peace,” comes three times: twice in ayah 9 and once in ayah 10. The whole section sits on page 516.

sections.title: No mocking, nicknames, suspicion, spying or backbiting; honour comes only through taqwā
sections.meaning: No group should mock another, men or women; those mocked may be better. Don’t find fault with each other or use hurtful nicknames. Avoid much suspicion, don’t spy, and don’t backbite: it is like eating your dead brother’s flesh. All people come from one male and female; the noblest before Allah has most taqwā.
points: No mocking, no fault-finding, no insulting nicknames; the unrepentant are wrongdoers
Avoid suspicion, spying and backbiting, like eating a dead brother’s flesh
One male and female, nations and tribes to know each other; honour is taqwā
sections.matters: Ayat 9–10 dealt with open fighting. This section goes after the quieter habits that poison relationships: mockery, labels, suspicion, spying and backbiting. Then ayah 13 removes the root of looking down on others: pride in race, tribe or lineage.
sections.story: Ayah 11 has several reports, such as a man taunted about his mother, and nicknames Banū Salamah disliked. Ayah 12 reportedly followed two men backbiting Salmān. Ayah 13 is reportedly linked to the conquest of Makkah, when some Quraysh sneered at Bilāl giving the adhan.
explained: Mocking, whether by men of men or women of women, belittles people who may be better in Allah’s sight. Lamz, fault-finding, is literally “don’t defame yourselves”, because believers are like one body, and whoever insults another invites insult back. Don’t use nicknames people hate. Once you believe, being known for such sin is a wretched name.

Avoid much ẓann, suspicion; some of it is sin. Don’t spy on hidden faults or backbite, mentioning your brother with what he dislikes. Would you eat your dead brother’s flesh? You’d hate it, so hate backbiting too. Then all people: one father and mother, made nations and tribes to know each other. Honour with Allah is taqwā, not lineage.
teaches: Never look down on anyone; they may be better than you with Allah.
Call people by names they like, not names that hurt.
Think well of others and leave their hidden faults hidden.
Backbiting is as ugly as eating a dead brother’s flesh.
Race, tribe and family are for knowing each other, not for pride.
sections.hook: Ayat 11 and 12 open “O you who have believed” and both mention repentance near the end; ayah 13 switches to “O mankind.” Page 517 starts at ayah 12.

sections.title: Bedouins claim faith but only submitted; guidance is Allah’s favour, not theirs
sections.meaning: Bedouins said “We believe.” The reply: say “We have submitted”; faith hasn’t yet entered your hearts, but obeying loses no reward. True believers never doubt and strive with wealth and lives. Would you inform Allah of your religion? Your Islam is no favour to the Prophet ﷺ; guidance is Allah’s favour.
points: Bedouins say “we believe”; rather say “we submitted”, faith hasn’t entered yet
True believers: believe, never doubt, strive with wealth and lives
Would you inform Allah of your religion? He knows everything
Your Islam is no favour to me; Allah guided you. He knows the unseen
sections.matters: The surah ends by turning to what is inside the heart. Manners, brotherhood and taqwā all rest on real faith, proven by steady conviction and sacrifice, not claims. And even that faith is Allah’s gift, so no one can boast of it.
sections.story: Reportedly about a group from Banū Asad who came to Madinah in a drought, declared Islam, asked for charity, and reminded the Prophet ﷺ they had never fought him, as if their Islam were a favour. Another report names bedouin tribes who stayed behind from al-Ḥudaybiyah.
explained: The bedouins claimed full faith. The reply: you haven’t truly believed; say aslamnā, “we have submitted.” Īmān hasn’t entered your hearts yet, and “yet” hints it may. Obey Allah and His Messenger and no reward will be cut. True believers never doubt and strive with wealth and lives: they are the truthful.

Would you inform Allah of your religion, when He knows all in the heavens and earth? They acted as if their Islam were a favour to the Prophet ﷺ. No: Allah did them the favour by guiding them to faith, if they are truthful. He knows the unseen and sees what you do.
teaches: Saying “I believe” isn’t enough; faith has to enter the heart.
Real faith shows in certainty without doubt and in sacrifice.
Don’t advertise your good deeds; Allah already sees them.
Guidance is Allah’s gift to you, never your favour to anyone.
sections.hook: Starts at the ۞ mark on page 517. Ayat 10 and 15 both open innamā l-muʾminūn, “the believers are only…”. “Favour” (mann) comes three times in ayah 17.

groups.text: Don’t rush ahead of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ in word or deed. Fear Allah, who hears and knows.
Don’t raise your voice over the Prophet’s ﷺ or your deeds may be lost. Those who lower their voices have hearts tested for taqwā.
Those shouting for him from behind his rooms lack sense. Waiting until he came out would have been better.
If a fāsiq brings news, verify it, or you may harm people in ignorance and regret it.
The Messenger ﷺ is among you; if he followed your wishes, you’d suffer. Allah made faith beloved to you, as His favour.
If two groups of believers fight, make peace. Fight the aggressor until it returns, then reconcile them justly.
Believers are brothers, so make peace between them and fear Allah, hoping for His mercy.
Don’t mock each other, find fault, or use insulting nicknames. Whoever doesn’t repent is a wrongdoer.
Avoid suspicion, spying and backbiting, which is like eating your dead brother’s flesh. Fear Allah; He accepts repentance.
All people come from one male and female, made nations and tribes to know each other. The noblest has most taqwā.
Bedouins claim faith, but should say “we have submitted”; faith hasn’t entered their hearts yet. Obedience loses no reward.
True believers believe in Allah and His Messenger, never doubt, and strive with wealth and lives. They are the truthful.
Would you inform Allah of your religion, when He knows everything in the heavens and earth?
Don’t count your Islam a favour to the Prophet ﷺ; Allah favoured you with guidance. He knows the unseen and sees your deeds.

1.explain: Lā tuqaddimū: don’t go ahead of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. Don’t speak before he speaks or decide before he decides, and don’t set anyone’s word above his. Allah hears your words and knows your intentions.
1.why: Reportedly Abū Bakr and ʿUmar argued before the Prophet ﷺ over who should lead Banū Tamīm, al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn Maʿbad or al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis. Other reports: people who sacrificed before the Prophet’s ﷺ Eid prayer, or who kept suggesting what revelation should say.

2.explain: Don’t raise your voice above his, or call him loudly as you call one another; speak with respect and calm. Otherwise taḥbaṭa aʿmālukum: your deeds may be wiped out without you even realising.
2.why: Reportedly Abū Bakr and ʿUmar raised their voices arguing over Banū Tamīm’s leader. Afterwards ʿUmar spoke so softly he was asked to repeat himself. Thābit ibn Qays, naturally loud, feared he was doomed, but the Prophet ﷺ said he was of the people of Paradise.

3.explain: Those who lower their voices out of respect have hearts Allah tested and made pure for taqwā, like gold tested in fire. They get forgiveness and a reward so great only Allah knows it.
3.why: Reportedly revealed in praise of those who lowered their voices after ayah 2, such as Abū Bakr, who vowed to speak to the Prophet ﷺ almost in a whisper, and ʿUmar, or Thābit ibn Qays.

4.explain: Al-ḥujurāt are the rooms of the Prophet’s ﷺ wives. They called from room to room, not knowing which one he was in, harshly and by name. That showed no sense of his rank.
4.why: Reportedly a Banū Tamīm delegation arrived at midday while the Prophet ﷺ rested and shouted, “O Muḥammad, come out to us!” One report names al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis. Another says they came to ransom captured family members.

5.explain: Had they waited until he came out to them, it would have been better for them, in this life and the next. Good manners are a sign of good sense. Allah still forgives those who repent.

6.explain: Fatabayyanū: investigate (another reading: fatathabbatū, hold back until sure). News from a fāsiq, a sinful or lying person, must be checked first, or you may harm innocent people in ignorance and regret it.
6.why: Reportedly the Prophet ﷺ sent al-Walīd ibn ʿUqbah to collect zakah from Banū al-Muṣṭaliq. Fearing an old feud, he turned back and said they had refused and meant to kill him. Khālid ibn al-Walīd, sent to them, found them praying and obedient.

7.explain: Allah’s Messenger ﷺ is among you; if he went along with you in much, laʿanittum, you’d suffer hardship. But Allah endeared faith to you and made disbelief, fusūq (major sins) and ʿiṣyān (lesser sins) hateful. They are ar-rāshidūn, rightly guided.

8.explain: All this is faḍl, a favour and blessing from Allah, not your own doing. He knows who is worthy of guidance and is wise in where He places His favour.

9.explain: If two groups of believers fight, make peace between them. If one keeps transgressing, fight it until it returns to Allah’s command, then reconcile them with justice. Allah loves al-muqsiṭīn. He still calls both groups believers.
9.why: Reportedly ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy complained that the Prophet’s ﷺ donkey smelled; an Anṣārī replied that it smelled better than him, and both sides fought with palm stalks, hands and sandals. Others mention a scuffle between Aws and Khazraj, or a feud over a wife kept from her family.

10.explain: Innamā l-muʾminūna ikhwah: believers are brothers in faith, wherever they are, loving for each other what they love for themselves. So mend things between your brothers and fear Allah, so that you receive mercy.

11.explain: Don’t mock: the one mocked may be better with Allah. Lamz is fault-finding; tanābuz is calling people by nicknames they hate. After faith, being known for such sin is a wretched name. Whoever doesn’t repent is a wrongdoer.
11.why: Reports differ. Reportedly men of Banū Salamah had two or three nicknames each, and the Prophet ﷺ unknowingly used ones they hated. Others mention Thābit ibn Qays taunting a man about his mother, Banū Tamīm mocking poor Companions, or women taunting Umm Salamah or Ṣafiyyah.

12.explain: Avoid much ẓann, suspicion: thinking ill of good people without proof. Don’t spy into hidden faults. Ghībah, backbiting, is mentioning your brother with what he dislikes, even if true. It is like eating a dead brother’s flesh.
12.why: Reportedly two men on a journey sent Salmān to ask for food. When Usāmah had none to give, they called him stingy, mocked Salmān, and went spying. The Prophet ﷺ said, “You have been eating the flesh of Salmān and Usāmah.”

13.explain: All people come from one pair, Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, so no one is better by birth. Shuʿūb (nations) and qabāʾil (tribes) exist so people can know each other, not boast. Akramakum, the noblest, is the one with most taqwā.
13.why: Reportedly at the conquest of Makkah, Bilāl gave the adhan at the Kaʿbah and some Quraysh sneered at his colour. Another report: after Thābit ibn Qays shamed a man through his mother, the Prophet ﷺ told him he was better than no one except by faith and taqwā.

14.explain: Āmannā, “we believe”, claimed full faith; they could only say aslamnā, “we submitted”. Either they were Muslims with faith not yet firm, or submitted outwardly only. Lammā, “not yet”, hints it may come. Obey, and no reward is cut.
14.why: Reportedly a group from Banū Asad came to Madinah in a drought year, declared Islam and asked for charity, boasting they had never fought him as other tribes had. Another report names bedouin tribes who stayed behind from al-Ḥudaybiyah.

15.explain: Innamā l-muʾminūn: the true believers believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and prove it by striving with wealth and lives in Allah’s cause. Ṣādiqūn: their deeds confirm their claim.

16.explain: Atuʿallimūna: would you inform Allah of your religion, as if He needed telling? He knows everything in the heavens and earth, including what is in hearts, faith or its absence.
16.why: Reportedly, after ayat 14–15 were revealed, the bedouins came to the Prophet ﷺ swearing by Allah that they were sincere believers. Allah knew otherwise, and revealed this.

17.explain: Yamunnūna: they count their Islam as a favour they did the Prophet ﷺ. Say: don’t. The benefit of Islam is yours, and the real favour is Allah’s, who guided you to faith, if you are truthful.
17.why: Reportedly Banū Asad told the Prophet ﷺ they had become Muslim without ever fighting him, unlike other Arabs. He said they understood little, and this ayah was later revealed.

18.explain: Allah knows the ghayb, everything hidden in the heavens and earth, even what lies in hearts. And He sees what you do, records it and repays it. No need to show Him your good deeds.
